extracted.intended_audience: young mathematicians preparing public lectures (colloquia, invited addresses)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for preparing and delivering public mathematics lectures (colloquia or invited addresses) to a general mathematical audience: how to choose content, organize it, present it on the board, and manage timing and audience interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: attract and inform
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of a public lecture is to attract and to inform; inform in a manner the audience can absorb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An attractive presentation with no content is worthless; a lump of indigestible information is also worthless. The lecturer should present material so that most audience members (who work on other things) can both be attracted to and learn about the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity (Less is more)
rubrics_metrics.description: A public lecture should be simple and elementary; it should not be complicated and technical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concrete: use simple special cases and concrete examples rather than starting with high abstractions. Avoid opening with deep technical jargon (e.g., 'consider a sheaf of germs...'). When a generalization is truly simpler and more incisive, explain it via a simpler 'cousin' example. Simplicity is the overriding principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concrete but don't lose the big picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor concrete examples and illustrations, but do not 'see the trees and not the woods'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listeners accept hinted generalizations more readily than on-the-spot abstractions; however, if the generalization is simpler and more illuminating than a special case, explain the simple cousin that makes the generalization clearer (examples: Artin, Gelfand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive explicit computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not compute in public unless a brief computation is decisive and illuminating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit computations (multiplying horrible expressions, carrying every epsilon) are often unhelpful. If a computation is decisive and short, include it; otherwise state 'it is easy to check' or give the outline rather than carrying out long computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive definitions and prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't try to make the talk fully self-contained by listing many definitions and theorems; detailed prerequisites overwhelm an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving 14 definitions and 11 theorems in 25 minutes is impossible to digest. Prefer selecting a few essential concepts and motivating them, rather than attempting to teach all background in the talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove something (or give the idea of a proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include at least one proof, lemma, or the idea of a proof to give the audience a taste of methods and why results are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving one little theorem or elegant lemma is valuable. If a full proof is too long, present the intuition or central idea behind the proof; this often communicates the subject best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention frontiers and unsolved problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Reach the frontiers of knowledge and at least mention something challenging and unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't confine the talk to only safe, known results. Discussing unsolved problems and the boundaries of the field helps audience understand current status and attracts interest; avoid being incomplete to the point of dishonesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize the talk (plan but deliver extemporaneously)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan the subject, order, and connections carefully, but deliver the talk extemporaneously to allow audience interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know your subject and audience; adjust the level appropriately (not talking down). Recommended structure: discuss three or four related topics and their connections, and break each topic into four or five portable subtopics so omissions won't wreck continuity. Extemporaneous delivery lets you react to audience cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust level to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the talk's level to fit the audience; slight overestimation is acceptable but too much will alienate listeners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's more important in a talk than in a book. Avoid insulting or overestimating; a listener can't 'put down' a talk like a book—an antagonized listener mentally leaves. Gauge audience and be realistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare content and blackboard plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare the subjects, their order, connections, and exactly what will go on the blackboard (when and whether it will remain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing everything out (especially board text) and running through the talk aloud at the board helps timing and clarity. Note: a dry run that takes longer than expected usually means delivery will run longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and respect for time
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep talks short; one-hour lectures traditionally last ~50 minutes—do not run over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nobody minds stopping at 45 minutes; audiences get nervous after 55 and displeased after 65. If you didn't finish, say so and stop; running on is rude. Prepare flexible material so you can cut gracefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chairman etiquette and initial positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect the chairman's role and beginning: give him a chance and sit with the audience beforehand rather than hovering at the blackboard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not float near the chairman worrying him; sit somewhere near the front with the audience before your turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a memorized opener to overcome stage fright
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorize one sentence—the opener—to get started comfortably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the opener, your preparation and knowledge will take over. This technique can reduce initial nervousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid annoying mannerisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid verbal, visual, or dynamic mannerisms; an annoying mannerism is anything repeated more than twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: repeated filler words ('in other words' pronounced oddly), elaborate fences around board material, teetering at platform edge. Try to eliminate repeated habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle mechanical trouble discreetly
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have technical trouble, signal the chairman privately and proceed silently to resolve it; avoid public bumbling or apologizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Say to the chairman only, 'I am out of chalk' or 'May I have an eraser?'. Make the appropriate silent decision and action without distracting the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use silence strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Short periods of silence after a crisp definition or theorem highlight importance and aid absorption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A five- to ten-second silence after major points signals importance; use this at three or four high points during an hour, but don't overdo it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board writing and speaking style
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak slowly and loudly; write large and slowly; do not write much—use telegraphic items, abbreviations, arrows, and key words rather than prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write things the audience can read as you speak. Avoid greeting the audience with a board already crammed with material; the visual growth is part of the lecture. Exceptions: pre-drawn pictures that take too long to draw may be prepared in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build flexibility into the talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare material that can be omitted or added on the spur of the moment without breaking continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two methods: (1) prepare two or three 'exercises' you can assign if you must omit discussion, and (2) prepare portable modules (omitable paragraphs/sections). Also prepare a peroration (three-sentence summary or list of key open problems) to avoid abrupt endings; when you stop, sit down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short talks require extreme focus
rubrics_metrics.description: 20-minute talks should be essentially a 10-minute talk presented leisurely; 10-minute talks must focus on one idea—the simplest non-trivial special case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice and time carefully; a 10-minute contributed talk should never expand into a 45-minute address. Some allow diving into the middle for 10-minute talks; others insist on extreme simplicity due to human capacity limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine fundamentals: simple, organized, short
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall rule: make your lecture simple (special and concrete), organized, and short; be sure to prove something and ask something; prepare in detail and make the talk flexible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember the lecture's goal is to attract listeners to the subject and inform them; 'less is more.' These combined principles summarize choices about content, organization, delivery, and timing.
